Droughts are caused by nature but water shortages are caused by bad politics.

Water shortages mean that water usage exceeds either the system capacity, or the available supply. As such, a water shortage is indicative of inadequate preparation. Since population and industry growth can be reasonably well-predicted, water demands can be projected for 10-15 years into the future over a range of growth hypotheses. This enables system capacity can be continually scaled to the upper-range of projected water demand.

Projected demand may outstrip available water supply. Overall water supply can be expanded by running long-range aqueducts from other locations, by expanding water-retainment and water-recycling capacity, or (more expensively and coast-dependent) desalinization plants.

Water supply is variable, depending on precipitation. Estimates of variability can be used to plan for worst-case scenarios. The aggregate water supply can be scaled to weather an extreme drought, defined as (say) lower than the 5% precipitation for 10 years.

The fact that both water availability and water system capacity can be tailored to worst-case scenarios which will effectively eliminate water shortages, it must therefore be the case that these projects are not a political priority. This is indicative of short-term, best-case ("brittle") planning as opposed to long-term, worst-case ("robust") planning.

Preference for short-term over long-term planning is a failure of human decision making; in other words, bad politics.
